title: I let Codex set up localisation and I'm not sure how to feel about it
author: muttsang
selftext:
Hey all,

Up until now I've mostly been using Codex and Claude Code to review my code, help me debug stuff, and bounce ideas around when I'm stuck.

For context, I'm a programmer with a full-time job and a family. I struggle to make time for my personal project and I usually only get a few hours on weekends, and even that isn't guaranteed. So sitting down to actually learn and implement a big system from scratch is really difficult.

Localisation has been on my "I really should" list for ages. My game has a lot of dynamically generated, joined and formatted text, and every time I looked at Unity's Localisation package I just got overwhelmed by it and I kept telling myself I'd get to it later. The game is still pretty early, but you hear over and over that you're supposed to set localisation up as early as possible.

So when 5.6 Sol dropped I figured I'd try something. Gave Codex access to the Unity project and asked it to set up Unity's Localisation package around what I already have, make it maintainable and easy to extend, and write documentation so future me isn't lost when I come back to it in three weeks.

It kind of one shotted the whole thing.

I asked it to add Spanish and Hindi since those are the two languages my wife and I can actually check, and from what we've looked at, the translations seem accurate too.

So now I'm sitting here thinking my workflow is basically, build the gameplay systems and content myself, and let AI handle plugging them into the localisation pipeline.

The thing is, this is the first time I've let AI genuinely "own" a system I don't fully understand myself. I've reviewed it, it works, it's documented but I didn't build it. And that makes me feel a bit weird. Not "I did something wrong" weird, more "is this how it's going to be now?" weird.

At work, of course I work in a team where other people are building a lot of complex systems as well but that seems different as that's not my personal project.

How comfortable would you be shipping a system built this way? Do you think you need to fully understand every AI written system before it goes in your game, or is reviewing + testing + documenting it enough?

And the Steam disclosure thing, since the translations that ship with the game are going to be AI produced, I'm pretty sure I need to declare it. But it's basically only code and translations, no art or design. Has anyone gone through this and seen how players actually react to that disclosure on the store page?

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
That's the neat part - localization is so forward facing it either works or it doesn't.  Text goes in, text comes out.  Did text come out?  Cool, beyond that *nobody cares* if it's the most elegant code in the world and it's not eating performance like a poorly written level loader that keeps shit way off camera in memory.

Where this will eventually bite you is when you go to plug in a language like German and now you've got text that doesn't fit in your UI because one random word is 42 characters long.  You'll need to have a plan to fix that (use a different word?  Dynamically stretch the text box? Different font?  Debug a hard crash?). But that's not any different from debugging anyone else's code you didn't write yourself.

replies.author: muttsang
replies.body:
nice thank you! it sounds like at some point I'll have to have some kind of human review and check for translations of languages we have for the game initially or outright just have human eyes on the translations from the get go once the system is fully up and running. 

Up until then, I guess we'll have to just put in a discolsure that the initial translations are done using AI.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
Honestly, it really depends on your project and the system in question whether or not just letting AI totally "vibe code" a system is fine or not.  Optimization is the big one, especially for 3D heavy games or games you want to release on multiple platforms, AI driven code might *work*, but it might also totally waste resources when you need to be conscious of performance.

For something like localization specifically, AI can absolutely build the scaffolding all on its own in any modern engine, you're really just making sure any text displayed anywhere in your game is a *reference to a key* and not hard-coded, which is no different than any other variable in the code.  For actually letting it *translate* the text?  Probably good enough for a rough proof of concept to make sure languages aren't breaking your UI, but I'd never let a single line hit production/release without it being edited by someone who speaks the applicable language.  It's far too easy for something to get mistranslated into something *wildly* offensive.

comments.author: Erandelax
comments.body:
Translated lines are exposed to the end users, sooner or later there will be someone who goes "this sounds weird in my language, is it AI translated?"

So with or without Steam disclosure, yeah, I would rather explicitly admit use of MTL and give users a way to report and correct translation errors in exchange for being credited in update logs or smth. 

And yeah, if I am reviewing someone's code, AI or not, I feel like I must understand what it does and how it works first.
Yeah the Translations are Generative AI so they draw the declaration, the integration with Unity’s localisation doesn’t though so only declare if you’ve done translation with GenAI.

replies.author: muttsang
replies.body:
Thanks! I think we'll just have to declare that AI has been used for translations initially anyways. 

Then if we might have to get human eyes to review and look at it and declare it as well.
I’d have no issue with it personally, I don’t know how godot work fully but I still let it handle the underlying engine and sleep fine at night
